LIBERAL PARTY LEADERSHIP CAMPAIGN-STATEMENTS ATTRIBUTED TO CANDIDATE JOHN TURNER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my statement today is about turn around, turn about, turn over Turner. When in government he introduced the Official Languages Act, but in Toronto, when making a pitch for the leadership, he cried: "Leave bilingualism up to the provinces". Later, when in Quebec, he stated: "I will continue the policies of Mr. Trudeau and Mr. Joyal in the area of official languages in Canada". A complete turn around.
Again, the ever turning Turner, when Minister of Finance, increased spending 99.8 per cent. He was an expert at emptying the public coffers, but now he will reduce government spending. Another turn about.
This hope of the Liberals, when in Quebec, said that he approved of Bill 101, that repressive, discriminatory piece of legislation because, he said, it is provincial rights. He introduced the Official Languages Act. Is that not federal legislation? Another spin around.
Our hero from Bay Street will reduce the deficit, but when he was Minister of Finance he introduced deficit spending and borrowing. As a result, Canadians now owe approximately $200 billion. Another turn about.
Guess what? The Liberals hope says that he is going to help the farmers of the West. As director of the CPR, he increased their freight to the point where farmers are going bankrupt. Even worse, he has again been appointed to the CPR board so that there will be another increase in freight to haul grain in July.
Will Mr. turn around, turn about, turn over Turner become Prime Minister of Canada? If he does, Canada will spin in circles. Heaven help us.
This sorrowful story will be continued on yet another day.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subsubtopic: INTEREST RATE LEVELS-EFFECT ON YOUNG HOME BUYERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Finance, who, I gather, is in Paris job-hunting, I will direct my question to the Minister of State for Finance.
In 1981 and 1982 thousands of people lost their homes because interest rates soared to an all-time high. Young people in particular were badly burned, and either lost their homes or had to delay buying homes. Now, just as they are regaining confidence, they see the same thing happening again. They see interest rates heading upward. They ask what is happening

May 15, 1984
Oral Questions
and whether they will have to put off buying a home for another five years. I want to ask the Minister what can I tell these young people.

subsubtopic: INTEREST RATE LEVELS-EFFECT ON YOUNG HOME BUYERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have seen an increase in interest rates over the last few months. However, they are not of a magnitude that merits comparison with the increases that we saw approximately two years ago. The Hon. Member opposite knows perfectly well that interest rates in Canada and the United States, both of which have increased, are still at a level which is very much lower than those of recent memory.
With respect to the question of the Mortgage Rate Protection Plan, which I assume the Member opposite must have in mind, she will know from an answer that I gave in the House a few days ago that it is our intention to bring in the legislation for the Plan very shortly. That Plan will provide protection for those who choose to participate in it. It will be retroactively effective as of March 1. The rates that were applying at the time a mortgage was either taken out or renewed after March 1 will be at the rates which applied at that time.

subsubtopic: INTEREST RATE LEVELS-EFFECT ON YOUNG HOME BUYERS
speechtext: The Minister obviously is not aware of the fear and the concern that ordinary Canadians feel all across the country because of the way they have already been scarred by high interest rates. They see it happening again.

subtopic: EFFECT ON UNEMPLOYMENT IN CONSTRUCTION INDUSTRY

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subtopic: EFFECT ON UNEMPLOYMENT IN CONSTRUCTION INDUSTRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there are approximately 700,000 construction workers in this country. Last month 200,000 of them were unemployed. They see a real slowdown in construction because of high interest rates. Developers are saying the same thing. People are afraid of losing their jobs or of not being able to create new ones. What assurance do these people have that if they start projects they will not have to be abandoned three or four months down the road because of escalating interest rates?

subtopic: EFFECT ON UNEMPLOYMENT IN CONSTRUCTION INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought that I had answered the question, but evidently I did not. I intended to say to the Hon. Member that indeed we do not anticipate major increases in interest rates in Canada in the foreseeable future. But whether such rates do increase, the protection will be available through the Plan I described a moment ago, which was embodied in the Budget of last February. The Mortgage Rate Protection Plan offers to those who choose to participate in it, for the payment of a premium, protection against the very circumstances which the Hon. Member opposite has described.
In fact we have seen some real progress in the construction industry. When the Hon. Member opposite presents her rather gloomy picture of housing starts in Canada, she should bear in mind that in 1983 housing starts averaged 162,000 units, which was a 30 per cent increase over 1982. In the first quarter of this year there was a 6.3 per cent increase over the fourth quarter of 1983. Therefore we do see some growth in
the housing construction industry. I am sure that the Hon. Member opposite will want to recognize that there is also the additional assurance of further growth in that industry through the use of the Mortgage Rate Protection Plan.

subtopic: EFFECT ON UNEMPLOYMENT IN CONSTRUCTION INDUSTRY
speechtext: What the Minister does not understand, and what the Canadian construction industry could tell him, is that every time interest rates go up by one percentage point, construction goes down by one percentage point. The Minister should also know that it is not only home owners or people in the construction industry who are effected; small business is also worried about interest rates.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there were 80,000 small businesses which had to close their doors in 1982 because of high interest rates, and people see the same thing about to happen again. Construction workers, home owners, and small businesses see a direct link between high interest rates and the unemployment that will result. They do not want promises from the Minister that have been made for three, four, and five months. They want to know what kind of action the Government is prepared to take to keep interest rates down.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member opposite must know by now, after having been in the House for the last few days, that interest rate increases in Canada are related to interest rate increases in the United States. That is an inescapable fact. Also there are some things we can do in this country to maintain moderate increases and to limit increases in interest rates. We can do this through increasing productivity, through the promotion of exports and, above all, through the reduction of inflation. On those three fronts the Government has acted, and acted consistently. We have moved to reduce inflation. We now see the CPI running at about 4.7 per cent, a low for inflation in Canada in a very long time. Second, we have seen record levels of exports which have been fulled by increased productivity in our economy, again as a direct result of some of the policies adopted by this Government.
We are in fact, Mr. Speaker, taking steps. We have succeeded in taking steps which do have a very real effect on limiting interest rate increases in Canada. But let us not be naive or fool ourselves. The basic reason that interest rates in Canada are increasing occurs outside our borders, in the United States. Unless the Member opposite wishes to suggest currency controls at our borders, then there is no way to avoid the longer term impact of interest rate changes in the United States.
May 15, 1984

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. Given the fact that it is now the stated position of the Government that the Government can do nothing about high interest rates, that the forces are outside our control because they are beyond our border, what advice does the Minister responsible for employment have for the Government to cushion the negative effects of high interest rates on employment in Canada?
We know that employment has not grown in the past three months. We know the unemployment rate is hovering around 11.4 per cent. We know that youth unemployment is on the increase, and we know that housing starts are down. We know all of these things. What we do not know is what the Government is going to do for the unemployed as a consequence of all this.

speakeroldname: Hon. John Roberts (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the general approach is still clear. The Government does believe that the private sector is the motor force for creating jobs in the economy. As the Budgets of my colleague, the Minister of Finance, have indicated, we have undertaken steps to create a context which encourages the private sector to create those jobs. Indeed, that has been happening over the past year. As the Hon. Member I think knows, there has been considerable job creation in Canada at a pace and a rate comparable to that of any other country, including the United States.
In terms of specific efforts, he has asked what advice would I give. I would suggest that we look at those programs which exist now, for instance, the Career Access Program which I believe the Hon. Member supports and, indeed, wants to see strengthened, and that in relation to youth employment; that we direct the young to use that program on the basis of support to private sector employers for the creation of jobs for young people and those entering the economy for the first time. There are a variety of employment creation projects under the administration of my Department or the Commission of Employment and Immigration-the Youth Job Corps Program, Canada Works Program, the LEAD Program, the Career Access Program, which I designed exactly to focus in on some of those employment problems on which the Hon. Member has just touched.

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister takes the position, and I do not quarrel with this, that the private sector is the principal vehicle for job creation. Let me say to the Minister that high interest rates are a disincentive to the private sector to expand. These high interest rates are happening at a time when there are over 500,000 young people unemployed, and that number is going up. They are about to be joined by another 400,000 young people from
Oral Questions
our colleges and universities, looking for jobs. That amounts to one million young people. If they cannot Find jobs in the private sector because the private sector is cutting back as a result of high interest rates, I ask the Minister what is the Government doing? Specifically, what is the Minister doing to cushion the effects of high interest rates?

speakeroldname: Hon. John Roberts (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
My answer, Mr. Speaker, has to be somewhat repetitive.
I am not sure whether the hon. gentleman was listening very carefully to what I said. No one, certainly no one on this side of the House, wishes to have higher interest rates.
He asked what was being done. I pointed out to him the Career Access Program. That Program does provide a contribution of up to 50 per cent of the salary or the wages of a young person, for up to six months and in some cases up to 12 months, to respond to that problem. We believe it is a much more effective program than the kind of tax deduction which the hon. gentleman and his colleagues have suggested, because the private sector employer receives immediately in his hands and at great advantage to his cash flow, les subventions, the subsidy, which will create a job rather than having to wait many months before having the impact of a tax deduction as suggested by the hon. gentleman. In other words, the approach which we are already using in the Career Access Program is a much more effective one than the alternative which has been suggested by the other side. It does depend upon the partnership and co-operation of the private sector, which we are finding increasingly we have.
The hon. gentleman asks what we are doing. The answer is the Career Access Program, which is an effective way of providing encouragement to the private sector to give a job opportunity to young people entering the labour force for the first time.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question today is for the Prime Minister. It emanates from a meeting which was held all day yesterday on Parliament Hill, sponsored by the parliamentary group on Soviet Jewry, concerning the situation of Soviet Jews. One of the recommendations was that a parliamentary committee be established on human rights to deal not only with human rights in Canada but internationally, including the situation of Soviet Jews, and especially that it would monitor the lack of respect for provisions in the Helsinki Accord. Would the Prime Minister tell us whether he favours the establishment of such a parliamentary committee, and whether he would at least give it serious consideration?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker I do not see personally why the subject could not be taken up

May 15, 1984
Oral Questions
before the existing parliamentary committee on external affairs. The suggestion has not yet reached my desk but I will be happy to see if the House Leaders want to examine that possibility.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is also for the Prime Minister. It concerns the same meeting. One of the other proposals made at the meeting was for more vigorous action on the part of the Government. Not only should there be quiet diplomacy on the issue of human rights violations, and especially the stopping of exit permits on the part of the Soviet Government, but this matter should be raised more vigorously internationally and in bilateral discussions with the Soviet Government.
There was some criticism that the Canadian Government had not taken what opportunities it could, and it had not been as active on this issue as other western European Governments had been. Could the Prime Minister comment? Could he give us any undertaking that the Government would be more vigorous in dealing with this very important matter of human rights violations and our concern that people, Soviet Jews particularly, be allowed to emigrate to Israel for purposes of family reunification?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: I would comment gladly, Mr. Speaker, but I am afraid that the comment would be to the effect that the suggestions by the Hon. Member, or by whomever she pretends to be quoting, are quite inaccurate. We have proceeded by quiet diplomacy, as the expression goes, but we have also made statements publicly and very vigorously. We have made them in every meeting concerning and surrounding the Helsinki declaration. We have made them in Madrid. Before that we made them in Belgrade and, at the United Nations in New York. We have made many statements denouncing the unjust treatment of various minorities by the Soviet Union and, indeed, by other countries. That does not preclude the need for quiet diplomacy. From whatever experience I have had, I think the latter produces generally more results than the former.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR DETAILS CONCERNING INTEREST RATES
speechtext:

The Minister has mentioned a mortgage rate protection program for which legislation is to be introduced very shortly and which will take effect retroactive to March 1. Could the Minister inform the House
today, considering the program's retroactivity, whether new home owners will be entitled to obtain interest rates at the levels existing on March 1 of this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR DETAILS CONCERNING INTEREST RATES

subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER PROVIDE MORE INFORMATION
REQUEST THAT MINISTER PROVIDE MORE INFORMATION

subsubtopic: INTEREST RATE LEVELS-REQUEST FOR PROTECTION FOR FARMERS
speechtext:

indebtedness in the $500,000 to $1,000,000 range. Every time there is an increase in interest rates of 1 per cent, their interest bill per annum increases between $5,000 and $10,000. Bearing that in mind, could the Minister of Agriculture inform the House what specific advice he has given his colleague, the Minister of Finance, with respect to policies that should be followed if today's farmers are to be protected from the Government's high interest policy?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: INTEREST RATE LEVELS-REQUEST FOR PROTECTION FOR FARMERS

subsubtopic: INTEREST RATE LEVELS-REQUEST FOR PROTECTION FOR FARMERS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: INTEREST RATE LEVELS-REQUEST FOR PROTECTION FOR FARMERS
speechtext: He really has no right to know the discussions 1 have had with the Minister of Finance concerning interest rates. Those discussions were private and confidential. speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):

subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF HEALTH SERVICES IN ALBERTA-REPORTED PRIVATIZATION PROPOSAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. By now the Minister will be aware of the fact that the Progressive Conservative Government of Alberta is consid-
Oral Questions
ering privatizing the administration of health care in that province.

subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF HEALTH SERVICES IN ALBERTA-REPORTED PRIVATIZATION PROPOSAL
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF HEALTH SERVICES IN ALBERTA-REPORTED PRIVATIZATION PROPOSAL
speechtext: I hear Hon. Members to my right saying "Hear, hear", that that is a good idea. That is interesting. Could the Minister tell us whether she shares our view that any movement in this direction, toward the privatization of health care administration in that province, would violate one of the five basic principles of medicare, that of non-profit administration?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF HEALTH SERVICES IN ALBERTA-REPORTED PRIVATIZATION PROPOSAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this point in time we do not know what Alberta intends to do. The press reports which I read upon my return from Geneva spoke of the Alberta Minister studying how far he could go in using private management in the health system. All I can say and report on right now is that we made sure-and all Hon. Members of the House agreed unanimously-that Section 8 of the Act contained quite a long definition of what public administration must mean.
It is a fact that Nova Scotia had a tiny portion or an element of its management done under contract by MSI, a private management firm. Also Hawkesbury, Ontario, had an experience with private management. For about a year I have known that the Governments of both British Columbia and Alberta are monitoring the situation very carefully. Perhaps it is because of the philosophy of those two provincial Governments that they have pilot projects in the same direction.
We all know that the next attempt at trying to undo medicare will be through the door of the condition called "public administration". For the time being it is strongly defined in the Act, and I have no reason to fear anything.

subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF HEALTH SERVICES IN ALBERTA-REPORTED PRIVATIZATION PROPOSAL
speechtext: This is not the first time the Minister has hedged on these kinds of questions concerning privatization. She did the same thing when I asked her about AMI at Hawkesbury last year.

Mr. Speaker, does the Minister not regard the contracting out of health care administration in any province to the private sector as a violation of the principle of non-profit administration? There is no need to be ambiguous about that. Does she or does she not approve of that direction? If she does not, what will she do about it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member displays the same impatience as he did four years ago when he joined the House. The net result of what I call the mysteries of life when I talk to him, because he does not seem to understand, is that it takes some time to know the facts, to collect information and to analyse the Act, the framework within which we must work. That did not preclude us from passing the Canada Health Act

May 15, 1984
Oral Questions
with a strong Section defining the parameters which keep medicare under public administration. I will not be governed by the typical NDP line that, just because a Minister was reported in the newspaper as thinking of using a private management company, this implies a sin of some sort. There is nothing wrong with that. Let us wait and see.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL AID TO VICTIMS OF 1983 DROUGHT

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Finance my question is directed to the Minister of State for Finance. The Minister indicated today that there is nothing his Government can do to separate interest rates charged in Canada from those in the United States. In light of that, why can we not have the same employment record as the United States? For example, in full-time employment we are down 4 per cent from mid-1981, and they are up 4 per cent. With regard to investment, we are down 20 per cent and they are up 10 per cent. Why can we not have the same kind of performance? We have their interest rates; why can we not have their economic performance?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member should realize that we in Canada have one of the fastest growing labour forces in the western world. The Hon. Member must realize that, as we create new jobs in Canada, we find that there are more and more people joining the work force, some of whom have traditionally not been members of the labour community in Canada, and others are joining the work force for the first time as the baby boom works its way through the economy.
In addition, as the Hon. Member should realize, we have in fact seen a further increase in employment in Canada. In the month of April employment grew by .2 per cent, a figure which represents about 25,000 to 27,000 additional jobs created in the economy. We are in fact experiencing some net increase in employment levels.

Mr. Speaker, the growth in our population and the growth in the number of new entrants to the labour force should increase our country's total productivity. The fact is that the Gross National Product is the same now as it was in mid-1981. It has not grown one bit. The fact is that the rate of full-time employment today is 4 per cent less than it was in mid-1981. The fact is that the American economy is on a roll. The fact is that the Canadian economy is still in a recession.
What policies does the Government have, from a finance point of view at least, which will turn the economy around? What will the Government do? Will it leave Canada to suffer with high interest rates? Is that the Government's entire answer? What proposals does the Government have?

May 15, 1984
Oral Questions

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Crosbie:
That this House is of the opinion that the Government of Canada can manage the economy in a way that would allow us to have lower interest rates than Canada now has and that we can have greater independence in interest rate policy despite the Government's failure to meet its commitment to so manage the economy.

Mr. Speaker, when the House rose for lunch I was at the point in my speech in which
May 15, 1984

I wanted to review the chaos that the policies of the present Liberal Government has brought to the housing sector.
Since the time of the Budget in February, mortgage interest rates have risen from 12.5 per cent to 14 per cent. That will add $50 a month to the cost of servicing a $50,000, 20-year mortgage. That amounts to $12,000 over the life of a mortgage.
The climbing interest rates have affected the demand for new home ownership and have reduced the attractiveness of building rental housing. In April, 1984 housing starts declined to 126,000 a year on a seasonally-adjusted annual basis. In April, 1983 the rate was 179,000. The important thing to remember about the decline in housing starts is that for every housing start that is lost, 2.5 jobs are lost in Canada. In construction, the unemployment rate in April was 22.5 per cent on a seasonally-adjusted basis or 27.3 per cent on an unadjusted basis.
The real tragedy of the chaos in the housing sector the Liberal recession was what it did to real people: the people who were forced to foreclose; the people who went through power of sale proceedings; the people who were forced to sell their homes; the builders who stopped building and the people who worked for those builders who stopped being employed. I suggest that during that time we saw social unrest in Canada, disappointment, heartbreak and chaos.
The tragic thing is that during the time of high interest rates there was no remedy from the Liberal Government. There were no measures adopted by the Government which would protect Canadians from high interest rates. We in the Progressive Conservative Party continually call for measures by the Government which would assist Canadian home owners. We continually demand that the Government stop bail-outs and come to the assistance of people with homes.
We noted with interest the remedies presented in the Budget. The Liberal Party now pretends to be interested in the Canadian home owner. We suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that it pays lip service only. What it promised in February has not come about by May 14. For example, in the Budget of February, mortgage rate protection insurance was promised. In mid-March the legislation was promised in a few weeks. Two weeks ago it was promised at the end of May. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that if the Liberal Party were really interested in the Canadian home owner, it would bring forward a measure to protect the Canadian home owner.
Let us look at what the Liberal Government did promise. It promised mortgage interest rate protection, and I am quoting from the Budget papers, "based on protecting the interest rate which was the market interest rate prevailing for the relevant mortgage term at the time the mortgage protection is taken out". In other words, Mr. Speaker, protection of home owners with mortgages as at the date that they file their application is envisaged in the Budget.
As a result of the questions which the Progressive Conservative Party asked in this House, the Government has now
Supply
backed down. It has watched mortgage interest rates increase from 12.5 per cent to 14 per cent and it has backed down. It has done that only because this Party brought to its attention the fact that if the Government stuck to what it said in the Budget papers, it would cost Canadian home owners 1.5 per cent on their mortgage protection. We in the Progressive Conservative Party take great pride in the fact that we have forced the Liberal Party to realize the damage which is being done to Canadian home owners by the very failure to bring in legislation-not to promise it, as was done in the Budget.
The Liberal Party also promised in the Budget to repeal Section 10 of the Act so that people who are now renewing their mortgages at high interest rates will have an opportunity to prepay their mortgages during the course of their mortgage term. I suggest to the Government that it is an interesting concept which would find a fair bit of favour on this side, providing we would get a chance to see the mechanics of it. Once again, Mr. Speaker, I suggest to the Government that the Canadian people are fed up with promises. They want to see the legislation.
With respect to the mortgage rate protection program, I suggest to the Government as someone who has practised real estate law for some time that I have a lot of concern for the mechanics of it. How is it going to work? The Government has told us: "Yes, we are going out to visit the banks. We will see five bank presidents, and based on what they tell us we will draft the Act". That is just not good enough for us in the Progressive Conservative Party, Mr. Speaker. We are interested in how that Act operates at the street level. Therefore, we will go out and talk to real estate lawyers and to real estate agents, because those are the people who deal with the Canadian home owner and the Canadian consumer. The Government worries about how it is going to go down with the banks, but I tell the Government that we in this Party have no concern about that. We are concerned with the people at the gut level, the people who are buying homes, the people who are being hurt by the policies of this Government.
Third and finally, Mr. Speaker, something else which the Government has only talked about in the Budget is getting into some set-up where we have long-term mortgages. I would offer the Government every encouragement to do that. However, I ask once again, where is this legislation? Where is this program? Everyone knows that is one of the problem with which Canadians are faced. They used to have 25-year mortgages, then the term went down to five years. Now they are looking at three-year, two-year, one-year and six-month mortgages. This is because of the failure of the Liberal Government to act. If it wants to put stability into the mortgage market, into Canadian home owners' minds, it will bring forward that legislation and it will bring it forward quickly so this Party has a chance to look at it.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I listened to the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. MacLaren) state, and try to prove by the very statement, that the Government has no ability to control interest rates or to build a safety net to help those people affected by high interest rates. Well, there is just no one out

Mr. Speaker, the other day in Saskatoon, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) said that if he were elected Leader of the Liberal Party he would see it as his job to put shoes on the baby and bread on the table. It seems to me we have seldom heard such a clear and succinct expression of the responsibilities of a Liberal Government. It seems to me that the expression of that sentiment sums up in one short statement the precise job we have to do as Liberals in government. It is our job, Mr. Speaker, to counteract unemployment, to cushion the most needy in our society, to stimulate job creation, to continue building a personal security network, and to encourage creative Canadians with new ideas for our future economy. We have done that, Mr. Speaker, through some of the toughest four years since the last great Depression. The Liberal Party has set those goals as our obligation, and we have followed and accomplished those goals.
The Tory attack on this record which we have been hearing today is a Tory attack on government help for business, for the unemployed and for those in greatest need. In the Tory speeches, particularly the speech just made by the Hon. Member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis), there is the impression that somehow we could insulate ourselves from the United States. In fact, that is the very spirit of the motion before us today. Since no one else around the world has been able to accomplish that, I have listened with great interest to see how the Tories would do it in our country. I have not heard any concrete proposals, although I do intend to return to the idea suggested to us by the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) earlier in the debate.
I want you to know, Mr. Speaker, that the Tory ideas presented here today are wrong. The world currency market is a fluid market. The United States is the greatest player in that market, a huge magnet, and we would be misleading Canadians if we told them that we could indeed follow the warped policies which have been presented to us today by the Tories. In fact, from now on, when we refer to the Tories we can call them "the little blue rump of the NDP". For years we have heard the New Democratic Party propose these ideas, which have been laughed at by people, including the Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson). That Hon. Member must be cringing at this motion today. The Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) sitting over there asks questions about setting up barriers between Canada and the United States. He knows better.
When was that?

I heard his question addressed to the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. MacLaren) today. What a terrible question that was. It left the impression that Canada could opt
out of the world. The Hon. Member for Mississauga South knows better than that.
On the weekend, Mr. Speaker, The Toronto Star ran a little article on whether Canada could lower interest rates. One official from the Ontario Government said yes. I needed guidance so I read that article with interest. I know the Ontario Tories are often responsible people, unlike the Hon. Member for Mississauga South who will say anything for a vote. This individual is reported in The Toronto Star as saying that we could lower our interest rates by three percentage points.
I read through that article with interest. I read his prescription for lower interest rates. At the end of the article I found that there were only two small price tags to pay for that. The first was a much lower Canadian dollar. The second was a little thing which he called a new tax on foreign investment portfolios which would, in his understated way, undoubtedly spring up if we were indeed to create a huge incentive to move our money out of the country. This man was going to tax that money out in order to prevent people from moving it. That is merely another method of currency control. That method would spring as many leaks as all the other plans which have been tried over the years. Let us dismiss this motion put forward today as the kind of pre-election politicking and hypocrisy that it really is.
We know that the Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre was right two years ago when interest rates in Canada and the United States were up around 20 per cent. At that time he said that Canada could not do anything different from the United States. That is still true today. That kind of honesty should be the real Tory policy rather than the sort of hypocrisy we have heard here.

Mr. Speaker, there are several characteristics of that management of the economy which I would like to discuss today. In our record you have seen a partnership between government and the private sector. That partnership is designed to create jobs and industrial expansion. That partnership was there in the recession, Mr. Speaker, when we provided help for vital but faltering industries such as Chrysler, Massey-Ferguson, Dome and the fishery. All of those industries came to the Government and with pride and compassion it was ready to respond and support them. in defence are all examples of the spending of taxpayers' money in Canada in order to get the benefit for our economy and to share in the new technology.
The first point I must make, Mr. Speaker, is that there is a partnership between business and the Government. This partnership has cushioned business. It has helped to revive and rebuild business. This partnership is encouraging industry and new jobs.

say that they would cut the deficit by some blanket amount are wrong and insensitive.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity today to add my thoughts and comments to this discussion and to remind the Government one more time of the effect that its mismanagement has on the economy and what it is doing in areas of Canada, such as Huron-Bruce. My riding is like many across this country in that it faces similar problems.
The speaker who preceded me, the Hon. Member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher), talked of many partnerships the Government has had with various groups in Toronto and across the nation. However, he failed to mention anything about the partnerships with agriculture. One thing is certain. We have to keep reminding Canadians that unless we have a strong a gricultural community, unless we have food, partnership means nothing for those people. Canada's food producers have been doing amagnificent job not only for domestic consumption but also for export. In particular, I would like to discuss the way in which the Government's lack of a strong economic policy is forcing Canadians to accept higher interest rates than they would have to accept if the economy were stronger. Through the Government's high deficit and its inability to strengthen our dollar against the American dollar through increased exports and equity capital inflows, the Government is forcing itself into a position in which it must follow the American interest rate policy.
This should not have to be the case. Canada should be able to form its own interest rate policy. We have the wealth and we have the resources. We should not have to suffer made-in-America interest rates. We should be able to strengthen the dollar and reduce the deficit on our own. By doing that, we can lower interest rates in comparison with other countries rates.
During recent years, high interest rates on farm credit have greatly affected the profitability and even the viability of farm enterprises. At a time when many farms have experienced a declining cash flow due to the decline in commodity prices and the increase in farm costs, interest rates have been a major factor in increased farm bankruptcies, foreclosures and forced sales. They have also been a cause of family distress in farm communities. The increased rate of farm bankruptcies is the most noticeable indication of the harmful effect of high interest rates. By the end of March, 163 farmers had declared bankruptcy this year compared with 115 during the same period a year ago. These figures do not include voluntary liquidations, of which there are probably that many again. This is something of which we take no account but of which we are aware.
While the Government keeps insisting that farm bankruptcies are not that numerous, considering that there are more than 300,000 farmers in Canada, many well respected agricultural economists argue that the number of bankruptcies of which the Government is aware is minimal when compared with the large numbers of undeclared bankruptcies. The Farm Credit Corporation estimates that a full 15 per cent of farmers are likely experiencing financial difficulty.
May 15, 1984

Bankruptcies are not the only problem created by high interest rates. Many farmers are forced to work full time off their farms while they continue to farm just to keep up with their mortgage payments. Many times members of their families are working with machinery even though they are too young to be doing so. However, with their commitment to agriculture, this is the only way they can carry on and perhaps meet their mortgage payments as well as their other expenses.
Even when there is no immediate threat of bankruptcy or bank foreclosure, high rates of interest on both short-term and long-term loans force large numbers of farmers to operate at far less than a fair return or at a loss on their investment. If they were to break even, many of them would be happy at the present time, given the general economy, with their equity declining and their losses becoming greater. However, food producers are generally unable to pass on to consumers their higher interest costs, so it is very difficult for them to adapt to rising interest rates.
Agriculture is a major building block in our national economy. For it to be viable, we need a strong national economy which will allow lower interest rates. Lower costs of money will not only help farmers but will provide relief ot all producers and consumers in the country.
A fact which is often ignored is that agriculture does not exist in a vacuum. Assistance to farmers and a recognition of their inability to handle increases in interest rates will help all Canadians. Lower interest rates to farmers and in fact to all Canadians will help small businesses, small communities, consumers in general, as well as small towns and cities. The hundreds of firms which manufacture machinery, chemicals and numerous other farm inputs would benefit if more farmers could maintain their existing farms or start up new ones. Many farmers would just like the assurance that they will be able to hang on to what they have. For retiring farmers it is very difficult to find new purchasers. The small communities which support the agricultural sector by providing consumer goods for sale would be more viable if agriculture were made more viable.
The point which 1 am trying to stress is that farmers are not just producers. They are very important consumers as well. They buy manufactured goods, often in the form of very expensive farm implements. They buy clothes and food which they do not produce. They buy farm fuels and automobiles. The list goes on and on. If such a large sector in the economy as the agricultural sector is forced into a situation where it is unable to purchase the consumer goods it requires, the ripple effects throughout the rest of the economy will be enormous. It has and will continue to affect small communities which are already shrinking in size.
A declining agricultural sector would also have a huge impact upon our exports. Agriculture now represents about 40 per cent of the Canadian economy and accounts for 10 per cent of our exports. We should be able to improve our export position. We have the ability to increase production so as to
Supply
become even more internationally competitive, but the economy must be strong if we are to do that. Agriculture has tried to serve better the international need for food. Our farmers have done a great job in expanding production and trying to remain competitive. However, they are being forced into uncompetitive positions because of the continuing lack of concern for the fact that farmers cannot indefinitely produce food for Canada and the world at unprofitable rates of return or at losses in many cases.
The Government speaks about finding new markets throughout the world, in the Far East or wherever. It talks about the need to expand agricultural exports, but it does not seem to realize or care that in order to expand our agricultural exports farmers have to be viable and have to be able to compete internationally on international terms. If our goods cost more to produce than those of the European Economic Community, for example, we cannot compete. With interest rates being a major input cost to Canadian farmers, any increase will further erode the comparative advantage they might already have.
Much of our recent trade performance has been disappointing. In 1968, Canada exported more than Japan. Today, Japan's share of world trade is twice that of Canada. We have fallen from fourth to eighth place in world ranking and continue to fall. With that decline, we lost jobs and prosperity.
While agricultural exports are not the only exports with which the Government should be concerned, their importance to our over-all balance of trade cannot be overlooked. Agricultural exports, particularly of western grain, are a major foundation of our national economy. They cannot continue to be eroded as they have been in the recent past. High interest rates and the state of the economy in general will not only hurt individual farmers; they will hurt all Canadians by hurting our balance of trade.
I urge that the Government examine seriously the effects of its high interest rate policy on everyone, not just on urban people. Agriculture is one of our most valuable natural resources. It must have the support of the rest of Canadians in times of economic difficulty. The Government of Canada, which represents the people of the country, is letting down the agricultural community. In so doing, it is letting down all Canadians who, I am sure, recognize how crucial it is to maintain a strong agricultural base.
I will turn now to the specifics of the Government's handling of those issues which most affect farmers. The Farm Credit Corporation recently increased its interest rates on loans to farmers from a flat 13 per cent to 14 per cent for a five-year loan and to as high as 15 per cent for a 10-year loan. I sympathize with the field workers of the FCC who have to discuss financing with farmers and food producers and tell them that the rate is 14 per cent or 15 per cent. That is not offering help. It is only offering a short-term existence until something else comes along.
I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) how he could accept or justify this increase at a time when farmers are facing more serious difficulties than other groups. The Govern-

May 15, 1984
Supply
ment claims that the economy is recovering, but the bankruptcy figures which I mentioned previously show that certainly the economy in rural areas is not much to get excited about. The Farm Credit Corporation and other lending institutions are moving on powers of sale, probably more than we have ever experienced before.
1 asked the Minister of Finance why the Farm Credit Corporation was charging 14 per cent on five-year loans when banks were changing farmers 13.5 per cent in the same circumstances and when home owners in the City of Toronto were obtaining mortgages at rates as low as 13.25 per cent. At the same time, five-year government bonds only pay 12.5 per cent. The Government pays 12.5 per cent for its money, then turns around and lends it to farmers at 14 per cent for the same length of time. I am alarmed by these facts because they indicate that farmers are on a lower level of priority than their urban friends. The Government seems to feel that it can keep that situation as it is.
The Minister of Finance responded in the House by saying that I had not checked my facts and that the rates charged by FCC were determined by how much the Government spent for its loans. He did not listen to me when I told him that the Government was not paying 14 per cent for five-year money. Also I was told in the House that the FCC was not making much profit. It should not be making a profit at all. Its mandate is to provide affordable financing to Canadian agriculture. I am generally alarmed over the state of the economy and over a situation which seems to be taking us back down the road toward drastic increases in interest rates.
We keep hearing that the increases in interest rates over the last while are not significant. We are told that they are so minor we have no reason to worry. The Government appears to be doing nothing to allow the Canadian economy to expand so as to become strong enough to have a more independent interest rate policy. We are told that nothing can be done about interest rates in Canada if American rates rise. We should be able to lower interest rates in themselves. The Government should be able to recognize that if interest rates do not come down to affordable levels, the country will be in a major crisis.
I have mentioned that the Minister of Finance seemed uninformed and unconcerned about the increase in FCC rates. I should also add that he appeared completely unwilling to reintroduce the interest rate rebate program which provided relief for many farmers during the last recession. Apparently he feels that such a program will not be necessary unless interest rates are over 20 per cent. I think he is wrong. When Ontario farmers alone are in arrears to the Farm Credit Corporation for $34,200,000, there is a necessity for some program of relief.
Another way in which the Government could help the agricultural sector right now is by swift action on the agribond issue. Again I must return to the biggest concern of all. While farmers would welcome and drastically need lower
Farm Credit Corporation rates, an interest rebate program and the agri-bond or some similar measure, the most important factor is a responsible management of the economy which would allow all sectors of the economy to grow and to be profitable.
The Government must be prepared to make the sort of difficult decisions necessary in order to get our economy on track. It must strive seriously to decrease its deficit by a serious re-evaluation of its priorities. There are many areas in which spending can be cut. There are many areas in which Government expenditure can be re-channelled so that it is more productively spent. This Government can and must strengthen the economy so that all Canadians do not have to be beholden to American policy. This Government must strengthen the dollar by expanding the economy so that it does not have to keep driving up interest rates in order to maintain the value of the dollar.
There is one last point I would like to make about agriculture and the impact of the economy on it. There is a great push these days for stabilization. Stabilization is a crucial factor in the agricultural sector and must be available and practically administered, but stabilization should not be used as a substitute for careful management of the economy. Stabilization should not be used as a factor by which agriculture remains viable on a year-to-year basis. Stabilization programs should be insurance programs against unusually difficult years. The economy should be strong enough so that pay-outs do not have to be made on a regular basis under stabilization programs.
The economy must be strong. It can be strong because we are a nation of wealth. If the economy is strong, the dollar will be strong. We do not need to have these high interest rates which are drawing us further into economic disarray.
I urge the Government not to forget the people whom it has been elected to represent. I urge the Government to consider carefully what it is doing to Canadians. I would like to add a special request, that the Government not forget the producers of food which feeds this nation. Canadian farmers deserve a more positive outlook than they are now encountering. If the farmers in this country are viable, we will all be better off. Farmers have a strong commitment to producing food, not only for this country, but for many other parts of the world. We congratulate the farmers who do that. They deserve a much better break, or at least the opportunity to be able to do those things.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the gloomy days of the recession, it was understandable that some people should make negative forecasts. After all, inflation and interest rates con-
May 15, 1984

tinued to climb, while all other indicators where we would have welcomed an increase, such as housing starts, employment, corporate profits and investor confidence, kept going down. It was hard to be an optimist. It was a real challenge to rise above the day-to-day problems of the recession, to remain confident and to remember Canada's immense potential and our own resourcefulness.
Mr. Speaker, the situation has been turned around, and quite spectacularly so, in many respects. Since November 1982, sixteen months ago, Canada has come out of the recession and made up for lost time. Canada has now made the transition to an era of growth and economic expansion. Unfortunately, there are people who have yet to change the way they react to improvements in our economic outlook. Mr. Speaker, there are still people who are so obsessed with what they see in their rear view mirror they refuse to look anywhere else.
You know as well as I do how important it is to have a balanced view of the situation when managing funds for which one is responsible. Only someone with a forward-looking but realistic attitude is able to assess, with any confidence, the risk associated with certain investments and the opportunities for getting a good return. Mr. Speaker, confidence is itself a determining factor in our economy. In fact, confidence can be just as profoundly satisfying as negativism. Conditioning ourselves for high performance through positive attitudes is not any harder than taking the negative view and letting our problems take over. I am not like some people who prefer to ignore the many encouraging signs of economic expansion we are seeing now, and who, for whatever reason, refuse to believe what they cannot see or touch.
Granted, some sectors in our economy still need further consolidation. However, 1 think more Canadians should stop indulging in this lack of confidence which is a typically Canadian pastime, and look at our successes instead. If we do, we will have some very real reasons to remain optimistic about our economic future.
Mr. Speaker, the best way to measure the consumer's confidence is to find out whether he is investing and where. Today, there are continuing signs that the confidence of Canadians is increasing. Canadians are spending more and more. The preponderance of automobile sales in the recent growth in the retail sector shows that Canadians have enough confidence in their economic future to make major purchases they would not have made during the recession or even at the beginning of our economic recovery. This increasing confidence is expressed in more than just a spending of accumulated savings. In fact, consumers now appear to be willing to borrow money to buy a car, something they would not have dreamed of doing only a few months ago.
Mr. Speaker, the increase in the number of jobs since the beginning of recovery has been exceptionally high. Since the
Supply
end of the recession, 418,000 new jobs have been created. The latest figures confirm that the upward trend is continuing. In April, 25,000 new jobs were created. These last figures are particularly encouraging, because they are a sign that the growth in employment is broadly based. New jobs have been created in most economic sectors and in nearly all provinces. These jobs are occupied by Canadians in all age groups. We should not underestimate the exceptional progress we have made in job creation just because the unemployment rate is going down very slowly. The paradox of slowly declining unemployment combined with rapid growth in the number of jobs can be explained by the increasing number of Canadians who are joining the labour force. We are all aware of today's extraordinary impact of the baby boom on the size of Canada's labour force. Mr. Speaker, as the economy and employment are improving, the number of Canadians who have started to look for jobs has increased. If our labour force was not growing as fast as it is, our unemployment rate would drop far more quickly.
Mr. Speaker, the increasing number of women who have opted for a career testifies to the remarkable capacity of the Canadian economy to absorb additional workers. In 1968,
2.500.000	women were employed, and nearly one-third of women old enough to work were in the labour force. In 1983,
4.500.000	women are employed and more than half the women old enough to work are in the labour force.
Exports are one key to a healthy economy. Canada's export figures since the recovery reflect an unprecedented performance. In the past year, Canada showed the strongest growth in exports of all industrialized countries. We registered a trade surplus of over $18 million last year, which is almost a record. We see a similar picture if we look at the tremendous progress achieved by Canada in corporate profits, the fight against inflation, the balance of payments, housing starts and so forth. This is very encouraging, especially compared to the recent gloomy scenario during the recession. There are, of course, exceptions to the general trend, but the trend itself is more important than the exceptions.
Nevertheless, some people insist on stressing the exceptions and playing on the fears of the public. I condemn those who make a habit of magnifying the exceptions to this sound and positive trend and blowing them up out of all proportion, as though we were on the brink of disaster.
Mr. Speaker, since March 1, the value of the Canadian dollar has been depreciating against the American dollar, at a time when all international currencies have been registering a very strong downward trend. For a better understanding of recent developments on the exchange market, we must see these developments within the broader context of recovery and the international situation.
The value of the Canadian dollar on the international market is determined by both international and domestic factors. As partners in a global economy, all trading countries

May 15, 1984
Supply
are interdependent, and Canada is no exception. Our economy is particularly sensitive to the changes and tremors that affect the U.S. economy. Actually, the recent depreciation of our dollar against the American dollar is due to tensions originated by our neighbours to the south.
American interest rates have gone up in recent weeks because the U.S. recovery has been stronger than expected in the first quarter of this year and because unprecedented deficit levels are forcing the American Government to borrow extensively on the U.S. market. The United States monetary authorities have admitted that the American economy had been forced into a precarious position as a result of structural and trade deficits. Indeed, Federal Reserve Chairman Paul Volcker has sounded a public alarm about the co-existence of those two deficits which are a clear and genuine threat to the continued growth and stability of American and international markets. Since it was feared that American monetary policy officials might decide to tighten up credit, and since there was growing doubt about a quick decline in the American deficit, their interest rates moved up. That is why interest rates edged up slightly in Canada and our dollar lost a few points.
I am not belittling the strength of our dollar, Mr. Speaker. If we consider all other currencies, including the American dollar, we can only conclude that, all in all, the Canadian dollar has remained quite stable. In 1983, for example, the German mark, the French franc and the British pound all went down markedly as compared with the U.S. dollar, much more so than the Canadian dollar.
It must be understood that the wavering performance of the Canadian dollar cannot be traced back to a weakness in our economy's competitive position. On the contrary, Mr. Speaker, the basic components of our economy which sustain our currency have always been and still are very strong. Our competitive position is gradually improving. There has been a spectacular drop in wage settlements and in the inflation rate, productivity is much better, and our trade balance remains quite favourable. The increase in labour unit costs has slowed down considerably as compared with that of the United States. Our trade surplus has reached record levels, whereas our American neighbours did report a trade deficit. Mr. Speaker, those are all positive developments which have sustained confidence in our dollar during the first year of our recovery, and we have every reason to believe that this confidence will be maintained.
Of course, our aim is to ensure a lasting economic recovery while at the same time leading a strong offensive in the fight against inflation. Mr. Speaker, it would be easier to reach that target if our dollar were stable and if interest rates were stable as well, or even lower. However, the upward trend of American interest rates has put Canada before extremely difficult economic alternatives. Any captain navigating through dangerous and rough seas has to steer the safest possible course.
As we proceed along our course, Mr. Speaker, we hear the voices of those who are so far off the mark in their interpretation of the current situation and who give us such injudicious advice to improve it that, if we were to listen to them, we would soon be shipwrecked. They believe that we should disregard the rising interest rates in the United States and try to increase the value of the Canadian dollar and cut down our interest rates. That is sheer fiction which can only come from a naive outlook on a complex situation and which smacks of irresponsibility. Such a view ignores the economic facts which Canada, as a trading nation, must take into account in spite of the unstable international situation. But what are these facts, Mr. Speaker? On the one hand, we know that sudden drops in the exchange rate may result in inflationary pressures which it is essential to avoid. On the other hand, substantial increases in the interest rates would of course offset downward pressures on the exchange rate, but at the same time, they would destroy our potential for economic growth.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of State (Finance) (Mr. MacLaren) have therefore clearly explained on several occasions in this House that we do not want to cause a major drop in the value of the Canadian dollar, as that would have inflationary effects and would also in any case eventually result in higher interest rates. However, we do not want higher interest rates either, especially at this stage of our economic recovery.
We must therefore determine what method should be followed to cope with the pressures which recently were brought to bear on the rate of exchange and on interest rates. I must specify that our method is first of all a response rather than a remedy. Indeed, the current problem with exchange rate and interest rate instability did not originate in Canada at all. It is therefore impossible to apply Canadian solutions. We may however minimize all of its consequences by taking a middle course between substantially higher interest rates and a devaluated Canadian dollar. And this is exactly what we are doing by promoting a policy of moderation with respect to both the rate of exchange and interest rates.
Mr. Speaker, this is the most serious and the most effective method that could be used. It is also the one which will enable us to turn the present recovery into a sustained economic growth. Moreover, it will allow us to maintain the progress so laboriously achieved these last couple of years in our fight against inflation.
As we are fully aware of the pressures exerted on the interest rates and coming from the United States, we are closely monitoring the situation in that country. However, I would like to allay any anxiety which may have resulted from the rather predictable panic brought about by these events. At the present time, there is no reason to regard the evolution of
May 15, 1984

interest rates as a tendency which will accelerate in the months to come.

speechtext:
The House resumed debate on the motion of Mr. Crosbie:
That this House is of the opinion that the Government of Canada can manage the economy in a way that would allow us to have lower interest rates than Canada now has and that we can have greater independence in interest rate policy despite the Government's failure to meet its commitment to so manage the economy.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-INTEREST RATE POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to be able to participate in the debate today. In the few moments which I have at my disposal I would like to concentrate specifically on a very important sector of our economy, namely, small business.
One of the primary reasons for which I entered the political arena in the first place some 10 or 12 years ago was my concerns as a small businessman and the problems which were facing this very vital sector of our economy. When I came to this Chamber, the word "small business" was almost nonexistent. But because of the efforts of many Members of Parliament on both sides of the House who came from business-oriented backgrounds, as well as of interest groups such
Supply
as the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, COSB, the various Canadian chambers of commerce and the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the importance that the small business sector has on our economy was brought to the forefront. Over the last decade, small business has indeed established itself on the floor of this House of Commons as a very important sector. Yet it is one of the most vulnerable sectors in Canada if government policies and government programs continue to affect it adversely as have the policies and programs of the Liberal administration during the past 10 or 15 years.
I would like to identify the three major problems which are affecting this sector: First, interest rates and the instability of interest rates, which is what we are discussing today; second, under-capitalization, particularly in the area of venture or working capital; and, third, government interference and involvement, such as government directives, controls and paperwork. There are solutions to the major problems facing the small business sector. I will return to those in a little while.
In the meantime I would like to address the point of interest rates and why it is so important that they be stable and, wherever possible, at the lowest possible rate in respect of small business. If a small-businessman does not know what amounts of money he will be paying for his loans three months from now or six months from now, let alone next Thursday- and interest rates can change on a weekly basis-he cannot make long-range plans as to his business operations respecting investment, productivity and other aspects of his operation. As a result, when interest rates suddenly start reaching unexpected highs-as they did in 1981 and 1982 when they reached record levels of 22 per cent plus-record numbers of businesses go bankrupt. When small businesses and businesses in general go bankrupt, unemployment starts to take place. Just when a recovery of our economy was taking place last year, suddenly this Government-which seems to be so insensitive to the problems of the small businessman-is again allowing interest rates to take off without any temporary or intervening measures to help or assist the small businessman in this country or to tell that small businessman what will happen to interest rates and what will happen to the economy.
We have changed predictions and changed budgets every six months. Business cannot operate under those conditions. The only thing that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) say in response to high interest rates is that it is happening in the United States. Why is it that in West Germany interest rates are at 7.75 per cent; in Japan they are at 5.7 per cent; in the United Kingdom they are at 8.5 per cent; and in Switzerland they are at 6 per cent? Why are government Members not saying that? Our interest rates are 4, 5 and 6 percentage points lower than interest rates in the United States.
The Liberal Government says that it cannot do anything because of the situation that exists in the United States. Let me ask the Liberal administration: How can it continue to plead innocence with respect to high interest rates and other economic activities? If, as the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance say, the reason for high interest rates in this

May 15, 1984
Supply
country is the high level of the interest rates in the United States, how come all the other economic measurements in the United States have improved dramatically when compared to ours? Productivity in Canada, for example, since June, 1981, has increased by 2.5 per cent. You may say that this is not bad under current conditions. However, it has increased in the United States by 9 per cent. In this country, full-time employment has decreased since 1981 by 4 per cent. Yet in the United States it has increased by 4 per cent. That is an 8 per cent difference. Residential investment in Canada has decreased by 15 per cent and has increased in the United States in the same period of time by 28 per cent, a difference of 43 per cent. Investment in machinery has decreased in this country since 1981 by a staggering 25 per cent. Are we the same as the United States? No, because in the United States investment in machinery has increased by 10 per cent. That is a difference of 35 per cent. Average business investment in Canada since 1981 has gone down by 20 per cent. In the United States it has increased by 10 per cent in the same period of time. Personal disposable income in this country, the wealth factor, if you will, has decreased by 2 per cent. Yet in the United States it has increased by 11 per cent. That is a 13 per cent difference. The list goes on, Mr. Speaker.
Therefore, if this Government says that we must do the same thing as the United States in respect of interest rates, why are we not doing the same with regard to unemployment, productivity, investment and all the other important major economic issues which affect every Canadian in this country?
Those clowns who are out campaigning for the leadership of the Liberal Party are not dealing at all with the problems which are affecting Canadians today. Within a month and a half, one of them is going to be sitting here in this House as Prime Minister, with absolutely no answers except to echo what this Government says on a daily basis to us in the Conservative Party and to Canadians.
We in this Party ask these questions of the Minister of Finance or, in my case, as the spokesman for small business and tourism, of the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Smith). Last week, for example, I asked the Minister what representations he had made to the Minister of Finance or to the Cabinet on behalf of the small business sector in relation to the increase in interest rates, which is taking place and which is so adversely affecting the small business community in this country. His answer is found at page 3594 of Hansard of May 10. I will read it, Mr. Speaker, and we will see if you hear an answer to the representations made to the Minister of Finance. The Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism said the following:
Mr. Speaker, the Government believes very strongly in the role of small business in pulling the country into a period of economic recovery. That was the main emphasis of the February 15 Budget. The Minister included a number of items in that Budget specifically designed to assist small business. Through the Small Business Loans Act over 25,000 small businesses in Canada got loans last year which they otherwise probably would not have received. I think that is a pretty clear indication of a commitment to the small business sector.
I did not hear in that answer, Mr. Speaker, any specific response to my question regarding interest rates. He did not say whether he made representations to the Cabinet on behalf of small business for which he is responsible in this House. Therefore, I read into his answer that he has not made any representations to Cabinet and does not really care about high interest rates adversely affecting the small business community in this country.
When the Minister in his answer talks about 25,000 small businesses getting a loan under the Small Businesses Loans Act, it is all fine and dandy, but at what rate have those businesses received that loan? I will tell you at what rate. The rate is 8 percentage points higher than inflation. That is at what rate. I have nothing against the Small Business Loans Act. It is a very good piece of legislation. I wish, in fact, it would be expanded to include working and venture capital. But surely, no matter what lip service this Government pays to what it is willing to do for the small business community of what it intends to do for it, if interest rates are going to continue to be allowed to fluctuate on an upward trend, nothing this Government can do and nothing anyone can do is going to solve the problems facing the small business sector and, therefore, solve the unemployment problem.
Canadians are becoming sick and tired of this Government attempts to deal with unemployment, for example by throwing billions of tax dollars into temporary and unproductive make-work projects. That is not where jobs are created, Mr. Speaker. Jobs are created in the marketplace, in productivity. The federal Government should not pay someone a direct grant in order to work him for six weeks or eight weeks so that he can then turn around and go back on unemployment insurance. That is not the way to deal with the problem. We must create a healthy economic climate in this country so that businesses, generally speaking, and specifically the small and mediumsized businesses, can operate in an economic environment which is free of government involvement and interference.
I asked a supplementary question of the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism about high interest rates and representations he has made, to which he replied this:
-it is very interesting to hear the approach of the Hon. Member. He is a well known believer in the free enterprise system, in market forces, in the law of supply and demand, and one who does not believe in intervention. The Government, however, does believe in intervention in certain areas.
The Minister is right, Mr. Speaker, except for the fact that when the Government interferes so much in the private sector and creates such a negative burden for the entrepreneurs of this country, temporary steps must then be taken to protect such a vulnerable sector until the economy has been cleansed of this tremendous negative effect caused by Liberal policies. That is why I said, Mr. Speaker, that there are solutions for those three major problems facing the industry.
There are various options to consider with respect to interest rates. Why does the Government not consider again the initiation of the small business development bond program? This is a program which would virtually allow a small business operation to borrow money through a chartered bank at roughly
May IS, 1984

half the interest rate. I am not suggesting that this should be a program which goes on and on ad infinitum, Mr. Speaker, but it is a program which certainly should be considered when interest rates are increasing, small businesses are being hurt, and unemployment, as a result, is growing on a daily basis.
I have already touched on the subject of venture and working capital. Our Small Businesses Loans Act could be expected to include venture and working capital.
The third major problem facing the small business community, of course, is government intervention and interference. Surely the time has come for governments, generally speaking, to make note of the fact that a business operation does not want Big Brother looking over its shoulder all the time. Surely the people who run governments today must realize that the private sector industry, small business or otherwise, is going to operate a heck of a lot more efficiently on its own than in conjunction with government. All one has to do is to look at the operations of Canada Post to see how efficient an agency it is, one which is now a Crown corporation. One can look at Canadair, for example. By the end of this year taxpayers will have paid out over $2 billion through the Government to keep it afloat. This amount is sufficient to cover the total liabilities of the estimated 10,500 small businesses which went bankrupt in 1982 alone. It is also four times the amount that the Trudeau Government has spent on various small business program in 1982. That is just to keep Canadair afloat. That is just one example. There are many others which the Government knows about.
The time has come, Mr. Speaker. It is long overdue. I said at the outset that both sides in the House as well as the New Democratic Party have established the fact that small business does exist and plays a major factor in our economic way of life. We have seen a sudden advertising campaign by this socialist rump of the Liberals who suddenly find themselves at 10 per cent in the Gallup poll. They are panicking their way into the hearts of the small business community, which is not going to accept them at all. All one has to do is to listen to some of the responses of the leaders of the small business communities to those advertisements. They know what the New Democrats stand for and they are not going to buy it. As I said at the outset, Mr. Speaker, the fact that small business is important has finally come to the floor of the House.
What has not taken root in the House is the fact that the House should not interfere in the workings of the small business sector. The small business person does not want government interference, regulations, controls and directives. He wants to be left alone. If we cannot establish an economic climate in this Parliament which will allow small business people to operate in a free enterprise society, then we must come up in the meantime with programs such as the small business development bond program. We must come up with programs like the Small Businesses Loans Act and expand it to include working capital. We must do those things until we can clean up the bureaucratic mess in which the Liberals have put
Supply
us. I know, as do the majority of Canadians, that the Conservative Party is committed to doing just that. We want to return the word "free" to enterprise so that the small business sector, the private sector, and Canadians as a whole can start producing and benefiting as a result of the policies of a true Conservative Government.

Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the House would readily agree with the Hon. Member that small business indeed forms the backbone of employment opportunities in the country. We have no difficulty with the analysis of the importance of the role of small business in the economy. However, I have some difficulty with the Hon. Notwithstanding the figures used for purposes of comparison with the United States, even at their lowest point, the number of housing starts in Canada has always been greater than that in the United States. Yet when the Party opposite had the opportunity of forming the government for a period of nine months, their consultant on housing made two recommendations. What is the Hon. Member's position in terms of support of small business in the area of housing? Is it to get out of supporting the private sector?
