Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member quotes a number of my colleagues. Of course, I have not seen these quotes. By the way, Mr. Speaker, I think we should keep our comments and questions related to interest rates and to the motion which we are debating today.
With regard to interest rates and housing, I think that if the Liberals and the New Democratic Party had supported what this Party had suggested while we were in government and thereafter, specifically the mortgage deductibility program, we

May 15, 1984
Supply
would be in a far better position today with regard to home owners with high mortgage rates than we are. As a matter of fact, it is my understanding that the Government is in fact considering something similar to that type of situation. As you know, Mr. Speaker, when the Government introduces programs which they have copied from us, we support them, as we did last week on the partial deregulation of the airline industry. That is an idea which came from this side of the House of Commons.
The Hon. Member quoted Members on my side of the House with respect to housing. I should quote to him the Prime Minister saying a few years ago that he would want to manage the economy in such a way that interest rates would in fact come down, because then the economy would be administered more soundly. Or I could quote to him the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) who said that he would resign his seat if interest rates did not go down, I have a whole series of quotes of statements made by Liberals which have been totally ignored by that Party and by Canadians. The facts are that this Party would like to see the Government move in a direction which would utilize mortgage deductibility programs in order to assist home owners in the country when they are hit with high mortgage rates.

speechtext:
I think he was talking directionally, not in terms of the correctness of my comments. I would suggest to him that the statements are right in the correct sense of the word and not in the directional sense of the word.
It is clear that the Opposition is saying today that the Government has, in essence, a policy of high interest rates which are exacerbated by the size of the federal deficit. They are saying that other domestic policies are causing the value of the currency to fall. That is the scenario that the Opposition is trying to establish today in an attempt to indicate that our present situation is the total responsibility and fault of the Government of Canada.
The Opposition is attempting to play down to the greatest extent possible the impact of external factors on Canada. We have heard very often that Canada is a trading nation which depends on trade for 30 per cent of our Gross National Product. Our biggest trading partner is the United States, which accounts for 75 per cent to 85 per cent of our foreign trade. This makes it difficult for me to believe that Members of the Official Opposition do not understand that we have a
May 15, 1984

very close relationship with the United States as a result of the extent to which we depend on the United States for our export trade and markets. If those Members do understand that, they certainly cover it up with statements that imply ignorance. We will need open capital markets with the United States so that that trade and flow of funds can move freely across the border. Otherwise, we simply cannot have an expanding export trade that will generate jobs in this country.
We heard a number of contrary views today. For example, the Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) indicated that perhaps we could free ourselves from the strictures of the international capital markets by implementing a speculator tax. Others have indicated other proposals to stop currency from flowing out of the country. The critical factor to remember is that without the ability of capital to flow between the borders of Canada and the United States and other countries, there is a reluctance on the part of those with whom we trade to undertake that trade.
Those with whom we trade must have the ability to receive payment in their own funds. For instance, when the Japanese sell cars, they would like to have Japanese yen in payment for those cars. Therefore, we must exchange Canadian dollars for Japanese yen. In that case, money flows out of the country. When we sell computer products, aircraft parts or indeed automobiles to the United States, that country will exchange their money for Canadian dollars in order to pay us in our currency. If we are going to facilitate foreign trade upon which Canada depends so heavily for our standard of living, we will need an open and freely flowing capital market. The simple fact that we depend so heavily on trade for our standard of living and our hope for a rising standard of living means that we should reject any notion that we can put strictures or constraints upon the flow of funds across the border.
Furthermore, one should consider the impracticality of attempting to apply exchange controls or a speculative tax, with all of the inherent administrative problems that they carry with them. I suggest that Members of the House should abolish that notion once and for all. It is not a realistic solution for an advanced trading nation such as Canada. It simply will not work. Rather, it would cause us great damage in our ability to conduct trade and generate exports. Consequently, this will hurt our ability to create jobs for the unemployed in this country for whom I believe we have the greatest concern.
If we are to have open capital markets, it follows that when the heart and soul of the world's capital market, the United States, undertakes policies that will cause interest rates in that country to rise, there will be a natural tendency for other countries to flow money into the United States to take advantage of those higher interest rates. Of course, this means that the interest rates in other countries will tend to rise or the value of their currencies will tend to fall. That is basic, fundamental economics. An analogy would be two tubs of water connected by a tube. When water is poured into one tub it will form an equal level in both tubs. Similarly, interest rates in Canada and the United States will tend to find the same level. Any attempt to keep interest rates in Canada substan-
Supply
tially below those in the United States will cause a leak and result in a drop in the value of the currency. On the other hand, if we make our interest rates higher than those in the United States, currency will flow here and the value of our currency will tend to rise. Those would be the effects if we were able to do that artificially. With an open and free capital market it is very difficult, if not impossible, over any sustained period of time to push one's interest rates below the rates prevalent in the major capital market country, which is the United States, or to hold one's interest rates appreciably above the rates prevalent in the major capital market country, again the United States.

Again we have a unique situation in Canada in that we depend very heavily upon the United States for trade, which influences our standard of living very heavily. Canadians are simply not prepared to take the reduction in the standard of living that would go along with any serious attempt to divorce ourselves from that capital trading market in the United States. Canadians will not tolerate it, nor should they.
Anyone who suggests these fancy, quick solutions to the interest rate dilemma in which we find ourselves or to the value of the currency situation in which we find ourselves is deluding himself or herself and is trying to delude Canadians into believing that there is a solution to the interest rate situation that is costless and painless. There is not. That should be self-evident, Mr. Speaker, and anyone who understands the mechanisms of international capital flows, the trading system in the world, will not put forward some of these nonsensical solutions we have heard. I think the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) understands that very well.

The Hon. Member for St. John's West, I think, has failed miserably in trying to make political miles with an issue in which he really did not have his heart. For the first time in history that I can remember, the United States this year will become a capital importing country. When the United States runs a deficit that verges on $200 billion-it might be somewhere between $150 billion and $200 billion-that is a massive deficit when it is compared to the savings rate in the United States. There is the Government borrowing requirement and a very low savings rate in the United States relative to most other countries in the world, and at the same time there is a very rapidly growing private sector-

If those savings funds are not generated internally by the U.S. economy, which is the situation the U.S. is facing today because of the low savings rate, then those high interest rates will cause funds to start to flow in from other countries. Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is simply wrong on a number of counts. The first area in which he is wrong is when he relates the United States deficit to the Canadian deficit without taking into consideration the differences between the U.S. and Canadian savings rates. The savings rate in Canada is at least three times that in the United States. In relative terms, the U.S. deficit is not half the Canadian deficit. However, when we compare it with the GNP, other personal income and so on, its deficit is slightly below the Canadian deficit.
The key figure is the savings rate. The fact is that Canadians are saving at a rate which allows the deficit in Canada to be financed without putting substantial upward pressure on interest rates domestically. Also, our internal demand for funds in the private sector is nowhere near as vigorous as that demand in the United States. Not only do they have large U.S. borrowing but they have a very large and growing demand from the private sector. At the same time, they have a savings rate which is only a third of the savings rate in Canada. That explains why our deficit has to be looked at in that perspective and why our deficit, while it is certainly substantial and needs to be reduced over time, is not the same problem domestically as is the United States deficit in that country.
When we think in terms of the over-all magnitude of the deficits in absolute dollar terms, a $150 billion deficit will be a massive drain not only on the United States economy but on most other economies in the world. This is because of the size,
Supply
in dollar terms, of that country's deficit and the amount by which it exceeds that country's ability to generate internal savings. That is the problem.
In terms of the trade surplus, yes, we have a trade surplus. Yes, we are doing well in terms of our ability to export and sell goods and services abroad. This is precisely why we have been able to hold our interest rates below those in the United States. We have generated export surpluses. We have done very well in that regard. Our industry is becoming more and more competitive. We are doing well in international markets. That has helped us to hold interest rates below those which exist in the United States for the last while.
We have suffered to some degree with a declining dollar. Recently there has been a declining dollar, primarily because we have kept our interest rates below those in the United States. This has been minimized by the fact, as the Hon. Member said, that we have a trade surplus. We are doing well in international trade, something about which the United States simply cannot brag.

Mr. Speaker, I have a sense of deja vu when I rise to speak on this day on this issue. I have spoken about this so many times that it becomes perhaps boring and certainly repetitious. It is, I think, the single most important question that faces us in Canada at the moment. It is the cause of much of our economic difficulty. In part, if not in whole, it is the reason why we have such high levels of unemployment. It has been the Achilles' heel of our farming community. It has resulted in bankruptcies of small business the likes of which we have not seen in this century. It has played havoc with the dreams of many people and families as they attempt to plan their future as best they can.
The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) says that having high interest rates is not the policy of the Government. I have heard that phrase on numerous occasions over the course of the last four years. The Government's policy may not be to have high interest rates, but it certainly has inflicted high interest rates on the people of Canada.
Everyone says that high interest rates are a result of the policy set by the administration in the United States. Listening to the debate, you feel that there is nothing we can do about it, that it is our lot to suffer from that policy, that as an independent nation there is very little if anything from a
legislative or economic point of view that we in Canada can actually embark upon that will in any way assist us. High interest rates in Canada have followed to a large extent the movement of interest rates in the United States. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), quite rightly said that our interest rates no longer follow those in the United States but in fact lead them. For some time they have led interest rates in the United States. Interest rates have been the main vehicle used by this Liberal Government to strengthen or at least stabilize the value of the dollar over the United States currency.
Every time we raise the question, we are confronted with the same answer: "There is nothing we can do about it". Frankly, I do not accept that. Although I recognize that any actions that we might take would be difficult and although I recognize that any actions we might take would have certain repercussions, the policy that we are now following is difficult and has repercussions. The one thing that I know for certain is that whatever the consequence of our actions, if we want to take actions to lower interest rates, they could not possibly result in more chaos or hardship for Canadian families than the policy being pursued by the Government today of following lock-step behind the United States administration.
This is not an anti-U.S. speech I am making. I want to make that quite clear. Frankly, I do not much care what economic policy the United States follows within the United States. I do not think it is much of my business what policy the United States administration decides to pursue in what it deems to be its own best interests. However, I do care when we in Canada do not have either the will or the desire to attempt to establish for ourselves an independent path that will result in some form of autonomy, in a fiscal and economic sense, for Canada in the future.
If we are going to pursue lock-step the policies of the United States, we are doomed to face these situations over and over again. If we are to tie our interest rates and therefore tie our economy, job creation, ability to house our nation, ability to deal with the question of financing for our small businesses and farming community, if we are to tie all of that to decisions of the United States at every single turn, the consequence can be nothing other than that if they manage their economy badly, we suffer, and if we make the wrong decisions, we suffer. That is unacceptable. I did not get elected to Parliament in order to accept without question the direction being thrust upon us by the United States. Neither did I get elected in order to try to satisfy the demand of the United States for additional capital year after year, as will no doubt be the case in years to come.
I know as I stand here that the people of Canada would be prepared, if need be, to take and hold certain consequences to themselves in the short run if they were assured that the Government had a program which would divorce us economically, to the extent that that is possible, from the fluctuations that continue to occur within the United States as a result of an administration gone wild.

The dollar is down as against the U.S. dollar because of a number of factors, not the least of which is the lack of economic activity in Canada. That decline in economic activity is evidenced by the fact that there are so many people unemployed and by a number of other factors. I put to the Hon. Member that if our interest rate policy were to create considerably lower interest rates, it would strengthen the consumer economy.
There is no doubt that if people could afford to buy homes, they would buy homes. If people could afford to take on such responsibilities at lower interest rates, they would take them on. That feeling was reflected in the growth of the Gross National Product. Although it was a small growth, that feeling was nevertheless reflected in the growth. We are now undermining that growth.
If we were to have a lower interest rate policy, it would inevitably result in a stronger consumer marketplace, and that stronger consumer marketplace would inevitably result in a stronger manufacturing sector, which would result in more jobs and more tax dollars for the Government. That would result in investors seeing activity in Canada and being prepared to put their money into that activity rather than into bonds or high-interest yielding papers. That would result in further economic stimulation, which would result in a stronger dollar. I suggest that that cycle is an intelligent one and it

They give another person a piece of paper that says "I owe you" and indicates that they are willing to pay interest in exchange for the money that they will put into something real-whether it

be a house or a factory, or something else. They invest in real things. When money flows into Canada and we give the people who put the money here a piece of paper, it is because we want the money to do something real. On the second point, I would like to ask the Hon. Member a question which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has put to his Party over the last several days. speechtext:

Canada's economic recovery continues to exhibit the strength which has made the North American recovery a world leader since the recession. From the fourth quarter of 1982 to the fourth quarter of 1983, real GNP rose by 6.6 per cent in Canada in comparison to only 6.2 per cent in the United States. It has been assumed that the firm but more moderate pace of growth of the fourth quarter will continue in Canada, unlike the situation in the United States where a burst of growth has been indicated. Yet our early figures for 1984 show impressive strength in a number of areas, including retail sales, manufacturers' orders, merchandise trade and, in aggregate, gross domestic product.
Recent indications of a firming pace of recovery in the rest of the industrial world are a source of welcome encouragement. For example, the United States Conference Board reports leading economic indices with annual growth rates at 13 per cent in France, 11 per cent in Japan and 9 per cent in West Germany, similar to the 12 per cent and 10 per cent readings for the United States and Canada respectively.
With more than 30 million unemployed in the industrialized nations of the world, job-creation continues to be a world-wide priority of some urgency. Canada is fully in accord with the need to build lasting solutions to the job challenge through encouragement of private sector expansion and the building of basic economic strength. As a nation which relies on exports for a significant proportion of its jobs, Canada shares fully in the commitment to international action to solve economic problems.
Canada's job-creation pace has been similar to that in the United States. However, our labour force has grown more rapidly. The result is a continuing rate of unemployment in excess of 11 per cent. Youth unemployment is of particular concern in Canada, as it is in the United States. We are projecting gradual but steady reduction in unemployment rates for all age groups, as well as a continuation of fairly rapid labour force growth in the years ahead.
Despite strong evidence of continuing growth, there has been an attempt by some to paint Canada's economic growth rate as faltering as compared to that of the United States. In fact, the recent edging upward of interest rates in both Canada and the United States reflects the concern that economic growth now exceeds a sustainable pace in the United States. This fear is, of course, closely related to concerns about the U.S. Government deficit and to the risk that overly rapid growth would create both rising inflation and rising interest rates.
Canada's competitive position has been improving since the recovery began, assisted greatly by a dramatic fall in the rate of inflation. For example, the rate of inflation, as measured by the GNP deflator, reached 3.8 per cent in the fourth quarter as compared to 4.2 per cent in the United States. Productivity has risen substantially. It is up 3 per cent in the fourth quarter as compared with a year earlier. Manufacturing productivity rose by almost 7 per cent, the best performance in 13 years. Unit
Adjournment Debate
labour cost increases have been moderating to a level of only 0.4 per cent higher in the fourth quarter over a year earlier, as against 2.5 per cent in the United States.
Canada's over-all current account continued to show strength in 1983 with a $1.6 billion surplus, the second highest on record. This is also in contrast to the experience in the United States in recent times. Clearly, the recent downward drift of the Canadian dollar against the U.S. dollar is not a reflection of a fundamental weakness in domestic economic performance.

subtopic: WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION ACT-TIMING OF PAY-OUT TO FARMERS. (B) PAYMENT OF INTEREST
WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION ACT-TIMING OF PAY-OUT TO FARMERS. (B) PAYMENT OF INTEREST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, amendments to the Western Grain Stabilization Act have been presented to the House of Commons in the form of Bill C-33. What a disappointment they have turned out to be. The New Democratic Party has indicated that it would pass the Bill as quickly as possible if that would guarantee a quick payment to the grain producers. Instead, the Government has come up with a series of amendments which will not allow a payment until November, or so. The farmers need some extra cash flow now rather than in the fall after harvest.
Also, the Government has not put into the Bill the specifics of the formula which will make the stabilization plan useful for the next five years. Instead, the Government has chosen the amount of $250 million and is busily designing a formula which will trigger a pay-out of that amount. In other words, the Government's concern is not so much for the farmers as it is about the money it will have to pay out. The Government wants to keep the payment as low as possible so that only farmers' money will be returned to them. In the last five years farmers have put in $300 million. The Government is manipulating the formula to ensure a payment of $250 million. Not only will the Government not return the farmers' money with interest, it will not even return the farmers' money. No wonder many farmers want out of this stabilization plan.

May 15, 1984
Adjournment Debate
My question is therefore a request for clarification, Mr. Speaker. Before the Government tries to push these amendments through the House, will it make the following guarantees? Will it guarantee to establish a secondary pay-out triggering mechanism that will be effective now, next year and for many years to come, and which will be sensitive to producers' needs, as it was intended?
Will the Government put into the amendments a retroactive feature which would allow payments for the 1983 calendar year? The Government could make this possible by an Order-in-Council. The Government was able to do that for the railroads. The Crow benefit was paid to the railroads before the legislation was passed and was made retroactive.
Will the Government put into the amendment an interim payment clause which would allow a payment to any time that a need is indicated and a pay-out is obvious?
Will the Government amend an initial deficiency in the Act and allow the Act to make pay-outs on a regional basis when the circumstances show such a need?
Will the Government arrange and put before the House, or the appropriate committee, an assurance that the cost of operation and its relationship to income will be a major factor in the decision to make a pay-out? Will the individual farmer's net income be a factor in the formula?
In establishing the formula will the Government also address itself to recognizing that there are problems generated by successive crop or market failures which would not otherwise be a problem?
Will the Government also add an insurance factor for crop or market failures for specific crops? If the bottom falls out of the flax market, it affects specialist farmers. The stabilization plan could trigger a payment for those farmers dependent upon that market.
The small amount which the Government intends the amendments to this Act to generate, an average of $2,500 per farmer, will not bail a farmer out of bankruptcy. However, it may buy the fuel or chemical for spraying or harvesting this summer or fall. This Bill could be a good start to an income security plan for the grain farmers. Will the Government move in that direction when it presents this Bill to the appropriate committee?

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Bachand (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION ACT-TIMING OF PAY-OUT TO FARMERS. (B) PAYMENT OF INTEREST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the question raised by the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo), I agree that making interim payments under the Western Grain Stabilization Act may seem attractive. Many western farmers are now short of cash, and it is true that funds to help them under the Grain Stabilization Program are available.
However, the picture changes if we take a closer look at the issue. First, interim payments are usually made when the present formula for calculating costs and income indicates the
need for such payments. That is not the case now, for the year 1983. In fact, that is why, on May 10 of this year, we tabled a Bill to amend the Western Grain Stabilization Act. The proposed changes should, we hope, result in substantial payments for 1983-84.
To be able to make these payments, the Bill must first be enacted. Furthermore, as the House is aware, the legislation provides that payments cannot be made until the end of the year, which will be the end of July if the Bill is passed in its present form. The new legislation was designed to accelerate pay-outs. We are, in fact, suggesting that the crop year be used instead of the calendar year as the period over which receipts are to be calculated. Thus, farmers will be entitled to receive payments in October or November instead of having to wait for nearly ten months after the end of the calendar year, as is the case under the present program. As a result, interim payments will no longer be such a vital issue.
We must also consider the administrative problems that would be caused by such payments under the new legislation. July deliveries may fluctuate enormously, and it is hard to make a reliable estimate. Furthermore, July 1 is the reference date used by Statistics Canada in calculating expenditures under this program. Final results are not available until two months later. Furthermore, it is difficult to evaluate the expenditures in these figures.
Finally, I may recall that if our Bill is passed, at the end of October farmers will probably be entitled to payments totalling about $300 million. Such payments would come at a time when most farmers are proceeding with major banking transactions. The approximately $6,000 each farmer will receive under the program would therefore be very welcome. That is why I hope every effort will be made to expedite passage of this Bill so that payments can be made at that time.

subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION-LIBERAL PARTY CAMPAIGN-ROLE OF CONTRACT EMPLOYEE. (B) MINISTERIAL STAFF GUIDELINES

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION-LIBERAL PARTY CAMPAIGN-ROLE OF CONTRACT EMPLOYEE. (B) MINISTERIAL STAFF GUIDELINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday, April 30, 1984, I posed two questions to the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) concerning the continuing involvement of one Jim McDonald in the Minister's Liberal leadership campaign as principal organizer or manager, at the same time that Mr. McDonald is also serving as a contract employee in the Minister's office as a speech writer. There is at least the appearance that the taxpayers of Canada are subsidizing, through the back door, the Minister's partisan activities. In this case it is his bid to become the leader of the Liberal Party of Canada. Such an arrangement between the Minister and Mr. McDonald is not only immoral but also against the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) guidelines on that subject.
Indeed, on April 11, the Prime Minister told the House in reply to a question from the Hon. Member for Durham-North-umberland (Mr. Lawrence) that there should not be any
May 15, 1984

involvement of any ministerial staff, permanent or otherwise, in a leadership candidates' campaign in any important way, in the Prime Minister's words, "without that staff either resigning or asking for a leave of absence."
The guidelines are clear enough. In the case of Mr. McDonald, he can either resign as the Minister's campaign manager or he can step down as a contract employee from the Minister's office. He cannot do both, but he is doing both. This is a clear affront to the law as laid down by the Prime Minister himself.
In response to my questions, the Minister said two things. First, he said Mr. McDonald is not employed in his office, but rather a company in which Mr. McDonald is involved has a contract with the Minister's department. Second, the Minister said the contract in question, though it will continue until after the Liberal leadership convention in mid-June, had been entered into by the Government of Canada before the Minister became a leadership candidate and it must now be honoured until the original expiry date. That was the claim by the Minister. He argued that the contract was with a company in connection with which Mr. McDonald had some activities, but that the signing of it was before the Minister became a candidate and, therefore, everything was fine.
There are two things wrong with the Minister's two-barrelled reply. To begin with, while it is true that the contract in question is with Mr. McDonald's company and not technically with Mr. McDonald himself, the reality is that the company is Mr. McDonald. The company is called Nunavut Communications, which is simply Jim McDonald incorporated for the purpose of his conducting business with clients. Certainly, he has a small staff, and in that sense, the company is more than Mr. McDonald alone. But the company centres on Mr. McDonald; it revolves around him. For all practical purposes it is Mr. McDonald himself. So the Minister was misleading the House in suggesting otherwise.
Moreover, any contract of the kind about which we are talking would have to be honoured by both parties under normal circumstances, as the Minister stated. No question about that. A contract is a contract no matter what might ensue after its signing. Any contract, however, can be broken or nullified with the agreement of both parties. And given the clear conflict between Mr. McDonald's partisan activities and the Prime Minister's guidelines-the incompatibility between the two-the Minister should insist that his campaign manager either resign from that post or resign from this contract position in the Minister's office. Mr. McDonald for his part, should oblige the Minister's order if only to preserve the Minister's reputation for personal integrity in the course of the leadership campaign. Otherwise we can only assume the worst, namely, that Mr. McDonald's contract arrangement is nothing more than a facade behind which he is hiding his true activities in the Minister's office and with the Minister as he travels throughout the country, at taxpayers' expense. His true pur-
Adjournment Debate
pose is the promotion of the Minister's candidacy for the leadership of the Liberal Party.

subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-NUCLEAR RADIATION EXPOSURE- DEMAND FOR EXPERT MEDICAL EVIDENCE. (B) CASE LAW-REQUEST FOR ACCEPTANCE OF PRECEDENT
VETERANS AFFAIRS-NUCLEAR RADIATION EXPOSURE- DEMAND FOR EXPERT MEDICAL EVIDENCE. (B) CASE LAW-REQUEST FOR ACCEPTANCE OF PRECEDENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 10, I asked the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Campbell) why he does not accept that there is a connection between nuclear radiation and cancer. In a supplementary question I

May 15, 1984
Adjournment Debate
asked him to accept the common law principles of precedent decisions and case law. Those two questions and answers were picked up by Associated Press of Salt Lake City and were published under a headline entitled "Cancer victims win N-test ruling". In part the article read:
A federal judge ruled Thursday that the U.S. government was negligent . .. and ordered it to pay $2.6 million in 10 cases where he blamed fallout for causing cancer.
The article continued, and in the last two paragraphs it noted what was going on the House of Commons in Ottawa as follows:
In Ottawa, Conservative MP Allan McKinnon, ... pressed the compensation claims of Canadian servicemen who developed cancer after exposure to radiation.
The Victoria MP asked Veterans Affairs Minister Bennett Campbell why his department continued to demand expert medical evidence from every claimant despite having recognized the link between cancer and radiation in other cases.
For some years Members of Parliament have been asking the Minister to take action to ensure that all Canadian veterans exposed to radiation at the nuclear tests in Nevada, or at the Chalk River clean-up, be located and the state of their health determined. Repeatedly the Minister has assured the House and these veterans that he was taking action in this regard.
The Minister is really putting us off with promises of studies under way and recommendations forthcoming. Last week in response to my question he said:
We expect to receive a total analysis of their case, and a recommendation arising from the study, later this fall.
This afternoon he said that the study would be ready in August. We are making progress. Perhaps, if we keep asking him, he will be able to produce a report within a week.
Meanwhile, veterans are suffering, and some of them are dying as a result of radiation-induced cancer. It is understood that the interpretation of the governing legislation, the Pension Act, follows common law principles. These principles are based upon the concepts of precedent decisions and case law. The Canadian Pension Commission has failed to follow these principles by requiring every veteran who comes forward with an application for a disability pension for cancer related to his exposure to nuclear radiation to establish, yet again, that there is a connection between his exposure and his illness. The Commission requires that the veteran produce expert medical evidence, from a recognized authority in the field, that his cancer is related to his exposure to nuclear radiation.
This should not be necessary. Not only is it difficult for veterans who live outside Canada's major cities to locate one of these recognized experts, but they should not be required to reinvent the wheel for the benefit of the Commission.
How many such veterans are there in Canada? My understanding is that 600 servicemen took part in the Nevada tests. Another 400 servicemen took part in the Chalk River clean-up. That makes 1,000 veterans who were subject to nuclear radiation. We need to know how many of them developed cancer.
The Pension Commission has the names and addresses of these thousand servicemen who took part, which I understand it received from the Department of National Defence. I understand that is nearly all of them. Others went around on training exercises teaching people to use geiger counters some 20 years ago. They were forced to carry cobalt sources so they would have something to test. If the Department is unable to get in touch with these 1,000 veterans, but is kind enough to give me the names and addresses, I will get in touch with them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question raised by the Hon. Member is an interesting one. The relationship between nuclear radiation and cancer has re-opened the debate, not only in Canada, but also in other countries.
The Canadian Pension Commission has already taken steps to obtain information on some aspects of the issue. The Hon. Member is certainly aware that the Commission is financing a study on nuclear radiation and its effects. The Epidemiology and Community Medicine Department of the University of Ottawa Medical School has been asked to carry on this study.
Under this contract a research team has begun to examine the impact of these factors on the death rate. The first thing was to find the members of the Armed Forces who had done decontamination work in Chalk River in 1953 and 1958, as well as those who had attended atomic bomb testings in Nevada and Australia during the fifties.
With the assistance of the Department of National Defence, the researchers were able to trace about a thousand people who took part in those operations. They were also given a list of veterans whose occupation, status and age were roughly the same as those of the people who had been exposed to radiation.
Mr. Speaker, a computer tape with all this information recorded was sent to Statistics Canada, where the data is now being compared with the files on the Canadian death rate up to 1981 inclusively. We hope that this stage of the study will be completed by the end of June. This analysis of the data by computer will enable the University of Ottawa to submit its report by August 31.
The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Campbell) and the Canadian Pension Commission had hoped to get the report some time ago, but it was very difficult to trace such a large number of veterans.
The Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) is well aware that, in the meantime, there is nothing to prevent a veteran who believes his health to have deteriorated because of
May 15, 1984

his having been exposed to radiation to apply to the Commission for an allowance. However, once this study has been completed, we hope that its findings will enable the Pension Commission to develop guidelines that will be used to process all allowance appliations related to nuclear radiation and its medical effects.

May 15, 1984

Your Excellency:
(or should I say "Madame", the title the French have used to address their Sovereign?)
It is a privilege and a great pleasure for me to offer you the best wishes of the Government, Parliament, and all the people of Canada on the occasion of your installation as Governor General. As your first official gesture, I would ask you to send Her Majesty, the Queen of Canada, a message assuring her of our loyalty and affection.
[English)
After being represented in Canada by men for such a long time, it is right and proper that Her Majesty should finally have a woman representative here. And I am happy and proud to participate in this momentous event, the installation of our first woman Governor General.
We are gathered today to celebrate a remarkable person but also a welcome evolution of our society. In fact, for this historic event to take place the natural candidate for the position had to be available at the appropriate time.
The time is appropriate, because our modern society is increasingly aware that women's qualities of mind and heart are every bit as valuable as men's, and that we need their fresh approach and commitment to peace and mutual support in order to establish a more humane society in Canada and throughout the world.
The time is appropriate especially because, for some years now, outstanding women have been challenging and conquering old taboos. With skill and determination, they have won access to the highest positions in the land. By freeing themselves from the restrictions that circumscribed their situation, they have inspired us to shake off our old prejudices and practices.
I am thinking here of pioneers like Emily Murphy, Nellie McClung, Louise McKinney, Irene Parlby, Henrietta Muir Edwards, Therese Casgrain, and many others who waged an uncertain battle at difficult times in our history.
I am thinking, too, of Pauline Vanier, Norah Michener, Gabrielle Leger and Lily Schreyer, who have a special place in the hearts of Canadians because their strength and unselfishness have left their stamp on their husbands' tenures as Governors General.
Lastly, I am thinking of all those women who have opened the doors of our highest institutions to their colleagues, women like Agnes MacPhail, who in 1921 became the first woman elected to the House of Commons; Cairine Wilson, the first woman to be called to the Senate, in 1930; then in 1957, Ellen Fairclough, the first woman to serve in the federal Cabinet; Rejane Laberge-Colas, the first woman to serve on a supreme court, appointed in 1969; Muriel Ferguson, who in 1972 became the first woman to serve as speaker of the Senate; Sylvia Ostry, who in the same year was the first woman appointed to a deputy minister's position in the federal public service; Pauline McGibbon, in 1974 appointed the country's first woman lieutenant-governor; Constance Glube, the first woman to become Chief Justice of a Supreme Court, in 1982; and Bertha Wilson, who also in 1982 became the first woman justice of the Supreme Court of Canada.
As the first woman to occupy the chair of Speaker of the House of Commons, in 1980, and to become Governor General of Canada, 1984, you stand in the line of these pioneers. During your remarkable career, you have accumulated probably more "firsts" than any other Canadian woman.
However, it is not merely to add to your record, nor because you are a woman, that the office of Governor General befalls you today. You have been chosen because, in the opinion of all, you are the ideal candidate for the position.

The role of Governor General is essentially one of rallying Canadians around the ideals that form the basis of our will to live together. .. and who among Canadians could do it better than you, Madame?
First of all, you represent all the richness and diversity of this country. You were born in Saskatchewan and raised in Ontario, right here in Ottawa. After completing your studies in France and Great Britain, our two mother countries, you pursued a career in Montreal in French and English television, with both the CBC and the private sector. Later, you travelled the country from one end to the other as a federal Cabinet Minister. And, as if that were not enough, as Speaker of the House of Commons you were called upon to preside over some of the most fundamental debates in the history of Canada, at the time of the referendum and the patriation of our Constitution.
This long familiarity with Canada has given you a great love for it, a love that, more than anything else, you wish others to
May 15, 1984

share. No one can hear you speak of Canada without being struck by your deep sincerity. Moreover, the warmth of your personality embodies to perfection the ideals of open-mindedness and tolerance, the spirit of sharing and brotherhood, that the Fathers of Confederation dreamed of realizing in this land.
These, then, are the reasons underlying your elevation to the position of Governor General of Canada. All Canadians trust in your talents to strengthen the country's unity and to embody, with grace and nobility, that ideal out of which the Canadian federation was born and which continues to inspire it. I am sure they will not be disappointed.
I wish to thank your husband and your son for agreeing to share you with us. I hope they will enjoy helping you carry out your duties.
On behalf of all Canadians, I wish you happiness and good health.
Henri Rochefort said that France had thirty-six million subjects, not counting the subjects of discontent. Give or take a few figures, the statement also applies to Canada.
Madame, may you find the words to persuade us that, for 25 million Canadians committed to live together, there is no subject of discontent that we cannot resolve in our efforts to build this country with honour, justice and respect for our diversity.
May God keep you and inspire you.

subtopic: REPLY OF HER EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL TO THE ADDRESS OFTHE PRIME MINISTER

speechtext:
Prime Minister,
In accepting the high office of Governor General of Canada, I will be honoured to convey to Her Majesty, Queen Elizabeth II, who has kindly agreed to my nomination, the message which you have entrusted to me, and with it, the assurance of the respect and affection of all Canadians.
I have been deeply touched by your words, Prime Minister. They have illustrated and emphasized your attachment to fundamental values and the importance which you place on the defence of rights and the assurance of equality. They are a testimony to the progress you have always sought to promote and preserve and to your love of this country. I also wish to thank you for having so sincerely and persuasively expressed your ideas on the significant contribution of Canadian women to the life and progress of our society.

In responding to that trust which you have conferred upon me, I follow in the footsteps of the multitude of women who, for 450 years, have served as the inspiration, and to a large degree, the artisans of this nation; those women by whose hands we have prospered and for whose spirit we have been praised. In the days and weeks ahead I will commit my efforts to the promotion of those ideals of unity, brotherhood and
peace. Even then, my determination and commitment are but a small fraction and reflection of the many gestures of good will and affection I have received, and to all 1 am profoundly grateful.
We live in a vast land of plenty which has never been laid waste by natural or political catastrophe. Though we have our problems, they are not as tragic as those faced by people who live in destitution, by the hundreds of millions of human beings pushed to the brink of despair. We go where we like without anyone challenging our right to do so, we say what we like without anyone imposing a totalitarian philosophy or system upon us. Each person is free to follow their own star, hold whatever beliefs they choose, express their ideas and opinions without fear; goods move freely, and each individual can share in them. We are not immune to human suffering, but in Canada it is not as deep-rooted and pervasive as the heartrending misery elsewhere in the world. Although we have to work hard, we do so in safety, and we have never been denied the right to hope.

It is for this reason that, from the smallest family unit to the largest gathering of our national community, we must forge a common purpose that will reinforce good will, bring together all our energies and proclaim the values we have inherited. These values are a reflection, first, of the achievements of our history, of the infinitely varied traditions preserved by our ethnic groups; in a more dynamic way, they are reflected in the long-standing effort by our nation to move along the path of modernization toward a humanism which will add to the common heritage so patiently and painstakingly built up over the years.
We have inherited a vast territory with well-established institutions, boundless resources and material wealth acquired at great sacrifice by those who have gone before, and it is our duty to fashion new tools for new hands; to go beyond our immediate horizons in search of a broader perspective; to scale new and as yet unimagined heights; and to move more quickly and surely toward the ultimate goal of expanding the potential of both the individual and the community. We must build in Canada a life to which people are not merely resigned but in which they will wish to participate fully.

Who are we and what do we wish to become? The answer is obvious. Despite our varied ethnic and racial origins we are Canadians determined to carry on the building of a great nation. We must go beyond even this ambition and aspire to set an example for the world by a deep involvement in global reconstruction, a reconstruction whose final objective is peace.
Peace is the ultimate goal from which we cannot digress as long as the world is inhabited by starving, mistreated people who are victims of the selfishness, indifference and cruelty of others. Peace should be our rallying cry, our foremost cause, and the most compelling objective of our common action.

May 15, 1984
Our commitment to peace must govern our state of mind and determine our approach to life and to work. This cannot be achieved in a nation of polarized thought and divided action. The desire for unity is, beyond doubt, the factor which inspires people to come together to create a truly human community.
In this spirit, we are fond of describing Canada as one big family. But what do we mean by family: a socio-political and cultural reality, an economic situation, a political status. All of these, of course, and also, I would hope, a common purpose to shape together the destiny of every member of the community. This can only be realized if we go beyond our borders and reach out to other nations to share with them the benefits of our efforts and research.
History and geography have determined where and how we live. We are aware how the challenges and obstacles they have provided have influenced our attitudes and our behaviour. What have we achieved through our efforts? I believe that after more than three centuries, our national character is beginning to take shape. All that remains is a final delineation of the traits by which other nations identify us. As Canadians in North America, historically and culturally linked to our countries of origin, we have won the right to determine our own future and to play a role on the international scene.

Should not our role be to return to fundamental values, to adapt to new ways of life, to review the basis of our private and public code of ethics and to utilize for the benefit of all the marvelous products of new technology. In approaching the new frontiers made possible by modern technology we must ensure that man does not become servant to the machine, but rather its master.
This, it seems to me, is a spiritual goal that can transcend mere insular nationalism and inspire us with the ideal of making the human adventure meaningful and filled with enthusiasm and hope. If Valery was right when he said "we now know that civilizations are mortal", we should also realize that each civilization bears within it the seeds of its own regeneration and transformation.
This is the reason I have every confidence in my fellow human beings and in man's potential and it is this that impels me to make an urgent appeal to my fellow Canadians to reach out to each other. If they would only remember that without co-operation, any attempts at communication and understanding will produce only meaningless encounters and temporary truces.

As we approach the end of this century, we are not immune to the crises that buffet our world and threaten its stability. The effects of this turmoil will be suffered even more tragically by the next generation; living as they will in apocalyptic times when virtually everything will be subject to question. We have made great material progress and worked hard to secure
this legacy for our children. We now have more money and more leisure time. Despite this fact, everything around us shows signs of impatience. Weakened by advertising, persuaded to claim, to demand, to receive and to take more, we act far too often like children who leave their broken toys to demand new and more exciting ones capable of rousing them from their state of torpid satiation.
Our mistake lies in our erroneous definition of humanity and the meaning of happiness. We have been seeking such happiness beyond the rainbow and it is now time to step back and reflect calmly, to take stock of our resources so that we can again set out on a voyage of discovery and find the meaning of the human journey.
When I ponder on the youth of this country, I am filled with pride and confidence. Their search for knowledge, their need for involvement, their dynamic nature and their strength of conviction assure us that in their own time they will carry out their role in determining the future. Their attitude shows us that they will be willing to accept the responsibility of mastering their own fate.
The day will come when they will replace us, when those whom we have tried to help will leave the paths we have laid out and go another way to build the city according to their own plans and to meet the new requirements of a new age. Would it not show an unforgiveable arrogance and lack of foresight on our part to try to forestall criticism of us at all costs by contriving to build and mortgage a world for the future which is not ours to create? There is a universal law that governs the progress of civilizations: one generation lays its stone, the next contributes another and, if the building material is always the same, the whole will reflect the vision, spirit and will of those who, one after the other, worked and died to build it. Although we have an obligation to build for future generations, we must not try to take their place and, in our feverish activity, give the impression that we do not trust them to be inventive and resourceful in their turn. We must prepare them for life, but we could be wrong to try to live their lives for them according to a model of our making.
As for myself, I have great faith in the youth of today. My past experience working with youth associations and my daily encounters with young people have revealed to me their spirit and potential. I am certain that when their time comes they will take up the challenge and shoulder it with success. As you yourself have said, Prime Minister, there are no insoluble problems, there are no situations that we cannot improve or correct if we unite our efforts; what we need to do is to talk to each other, to work together intelligently and honestly and let time, "the great sculptor", as Marguerite Yourcenar has so aptly put it, shape and refine the structure of our Canadian federation.

I believe in the strength of our people, in our collective strength, and in the power to recreate society through the practice of those time-tested virtues that have always led
May 15, 1984

people to surpass themselves and give the full measure of their faith, wisdom and courage. We must practise these virtues together. My task, which I take on publicly before you, is to become better acquainted with my countrymen, to meet with them, to seek them out wherever they are in this great land, and to instil in them the confidence that makes and seals destinies. Our common task is to promote tolerance, to help each other, and to reject imitations of freedom. This is the price of our happiness, but happiness will never be found in the spirit of "every man for himself'; it requires that we share our good fortune as Canadians so that we might benefit the many peoples of the world.
To carry out my duties, I need the help of each and every one of you now and in the future. We must be united in spirit if we are to go forward in unity and brotherhood on the exhilarating road that Providence has so generously laid out before us. As Ecclesiasticus says:
"... as the governor is, so will be the inhabitants of his city." (Eccl. 10:2)
I ask for your support in the days ahead. We share with each other a common inspiration for we have all at one time experienced the eternal truth expressed in the words of the psalm:
"If Yaweh does not build the house, in vain the masons toil..." (Ps. 127:1)
Wednesday, May 16, 1984
